newsitem.title: PERU: Peru rebels reply to police moves by firing in air.
newsitem.headline: Peru rebels reply to police moves by firing in air.

text.p: Marxist rebels holding 73 VIP hostages for a 39th day fired two warning shots into the air on Saturday in response to police manoeuvres around the besieged Japanese ambassador's residence.
The gunfire sent journalists scurrying for cover and put police on alert. They crouched and trained their guns on the fortified compound.
"They (the rebels) simply fired into the air. I do not know why," said a police officer on patrol two blocks from the residence.
On hearing the gunshots, two special forces police rushed a side door of the compound and appeared to listen to activity inside, witnesses said.

"We ask for calm so as not to put any lives at risk," Red Cross representative Ruben Ortega said. The Red Cross, which entered the building half an hour after the shots, said it was too early to give details about the shots.

The Tupac Amaru Revolutionary Movement (MRTA) rebels have periodically fired warning shots into the air during the 39 days in response to police moves close to the building. The shots have caused no injuries.
Earlier on Saturday, the MRTA accused the government of preparing for a storming of the besieged home by staging military operations around the building.

Armoured vehicles have rolled up to the residence on two occasions, while a police helicopter has been flying overhead and troops have periodically taken up positions around the perimeter wall with guns trained on the building.
The helicopter again made several passes over the building on Saturday, including after the shooting.
But in apparent concerted efforts to calm nerves at the site, the government pledged on Saturday it would ensure a peaceful solution to the crisis, despite the police manoeuvres.
"We are going to take the time needed to reach a peaceful solution to this crisis without bloodshed," Prime Minister Alberto Pandolfi told reporters.
Pandolfi gave no evidence, however, that talks were imminent. They have stalled over the government's refusal to consider the MRTA's main demand for the release of some 400 jailed comrades.

President Alberto Fujimori also sought to defuse tensions, insisting the police were merely doing their job of patrolling and called for calm. "What we need is a period with not much talking but time for everyone to reflect," he told a news conference after a two-hour meeting with his negotiator, Domingo Palermo.
Despite the government's hard line on the prisoners, Fujimori has offered the roughly 15 heavily armed rebels safe passage to a foreign country, provided they lay down arms and release the hostages.
Palermo, however, revealed he had held a preliminary meeting with a commission of "guarantors" who will oversee eventual talks, and insisted there was hope.
"The Red Cross is preparing for the MRTA to eventually come out for the start of conversations," he said. "I am going to be very clear. There is no deadlock. There is a prudent reserve."
An armoured personnel carrier approached the main entrance at 10:30 p.m. on Friday (0330 GMT Saturday) with special forces police on board training their rifles and machine guns on the residence.

Eight policemen, armed with assault rifles and night vision goggles, also rushed toward the compound's main entrance and crouched on either side training their guns on the building. Red laser beams were seen cutting across the garden to the house.

In a two-way radio conversation monitored by the local Radio Programas del Peru radio station, a man identifying himself as MRTA leader Nestor Cerpa Cartolini said the activity had frightened the hostages but did not bother the rebels.
